functional.text: A merchant creates a payment: charge a customer's payment method for an amount and currency.
Merchants query payment status and receive webhooks on every state change.
Refunds (full or partial); merchant balances are tracked for payouts.
Reconcile daily with the processor's settlement reports.

non_functional.text: Exactly-once effect: no retry (merchant, ours or the PSP's) ever charges twice.
Correctness over availability: every money movement is in a balanced, immutable ledger, auditable to the cent.
99.99% available payment API; p99 < 3 s including the processor.
Keep the financial history for 7 years.

assumptions.text: 10M payments/day, ~10× peak on Black Friday; ~6 ledger entries per payment over its life.
Card data is tokenized by the processor (PSP); we never store card numbers.

out_of_scope.text: Fraud scoring, currency conversion, card network internals, the merchant dashboard.

api.request: amount, currency, payment_method (token), order_id; Idempotency-Key header

api.notes: Same state machine and PSP path.
Deduped by PSP event id; moves the state machine.

data.name: payments
data.fields: payment_id (PK), merchant_id, amount, currency, status created|pending|unknown|succeeded|failed|refunded, psp_ref, attempts, version
data.why: Transactional state machine; sharded by merchant_id.

data.name: idempotency_keys
data.fields: (merchant_id, key) unique, request_hash, state, response, expires_at
data.why: Same database and transaction as the payment row.

data.name: ledger_entries
data.fields: entry_id, txn_id, account_id, direction debit|credit, amount, currency, source_event_id (unique), created_at
data.why: Append-only double-entry ledger; debits = credits per txn_id; partitioned by month.

data.name: accounts
data.why: Balances are derived from entries and cached.

data.name: outbox
data.why: Committed with the state change; relayed to Kafka.

data.name: settlement files
data.fields: raw PSP reports + reconciliation results per day

deep_dives.title: A PSP call times out: unknown outcome

options.name: Treat as failed and let the merchant retry
options.cons: the customer may have been charged: a retry double charges unless the key is reused

options.name: Mark 'unknown', query the PSP by our payment_id, wait for the webhook, retry only with the same key
options.cons: the merchant sees 'pending' for a while

deep_dives.choice: Mark the payment unknown, return 202 pending, resolve by status query and webhook; retries reuse the same PSP idempotency key; reconciliation is the backstop
deep_dives.why: N1: a timeout is not a failure. The only safe actions are ones that are idempotent at the PSP.

deep_dives.title: Getting payment state into the ledger

options.name: 2PC across the payments DB and the ledger DB
options.cons: coordinator blocking, poor availability, few tools support it

options.name: Dual write from the service
options.cons: a crash between writes loses or duplicates a posting

options.name: Transactional outbox → Kafka → idempotent ledger poster
options.pros: no lost or double postings; services decoupled
options.cons: the ledger lags by seconds

deep_dives.choice: Transactional outbox → Kafka → ledger poster with a unique source_event_id
deep_dives.why: N2 needs every posting exactly once; a unique event id turns at-least-once delivery into exactly-once effect without a distributed transaction.

deep_dives.title: Correcting mistakes in the ledger

options.name: UPDATE or DELETE the wrong entries
options.cons: destroys the audit trail

options.name: Post reversing entries plus new correct entries
options.cons: more rows

deep_dives.choice: Never edit: post reversing and correcting entries
deep_dives.why: N2 and N4: auditors must be able to replay every balance at any date.

wrapup.bottlenecks: The processor (latency and rate limits; mitigated with multiple PSPs and circuit breakers), hot merchant rows on one shard during a flash sale, and the ledger's hottest accounts (fees, PSP receivable), handled by sharding them into sub-accounts and summing.
wrapup.failures: PSP outage: circuit breaker, new payments routed to a second PSP, pending ones retried with backoff, DLQ after N tries for manual review. Lost webhook: executor status polling and reconciliation. Ledger DB down: events wait in Kafka, payments continue, postings catch up. Relay down: outbox rows accumulate, nothing is lost.
wrapup.monitoring: Authorization success/decline rate per PSP, p99 latency, payments stuck in pending/unknown > 5 min, retry queue depth and DLQ size, relay and poster lag, ledger imbalance (sum of entries must be exactly 0), reconciliation breaks per day.
wrapup.scale: Shard payments by merchant_id and the ledger by account and month; add executors for PSP concurrency; partition Kafka by payment_id to keep each payment's events ordered.
wrapup.future: Multi-currency with FX entries, smart routing across PSPs by cost and success rate, risk scoring before authorization, instant payouts.

parts.title: Idempotent payment API
parts.problem: Merchants retry after timeouts and network errors. The same request must have the same effect and get the same answer, even if the first attempt is still in flight; no duplicate charges.

options.name: No idempotency; rely on clients not retrying
options.cons: every timeout risks a double charge

options.name: Dedupe on a natural key (merchant, order_id)
options.cons: a legitimate second charge for the same order is blocked; not every call has an order id

options.name: Idempotency keys cached in Redis
options.cons: a failover loses keys exactly when retries spike; not atomic with the payment row

options.name: Idempotency-Key table in Postgres, written in the payment's own transaction
options.pros: atomic with the effect; durable; stores the response to replay
options.cons: a unique-index write per request

parts.choice: Idempotency-Key table in Postgres: (merchant_id, key) unique, with request hash, state and stored response, written in the same transaction as the payment row
parts.why: At ~1,200 payments/s peak an extra indexed insert is trivial, and only a key that commits atomically with the payment can guarantee N1. Same key + different body → 422; same key while in flight → 409; finished → replay the stored response.

nodes.label: Payments DB: payments, idempotency keys, outbox

parts.title: Payment state machine and PSP calls with retries
parts.problem: The external processor takes 1–3 s, fails transiently, and sometimes times out with the outcome unknown. Drive each payment to a final state without ever charging twice.

options.name: Call the PSP synchronously and retry blindly on errors
options.cons: a timeout + retry can charge twice; no record of what was attempted

options.name: Persisted state machine; PSP called with our payment_id as its idempotency key; retryable errors to a backoff queue; unknowns resolved by status query and webhook
options.pros: every retry is safe; crash-recoverable; no stuck payments
options.cons: more states (pending, unknown) and a worker pool to run

parts.choice: Persisted state machine (created → pending → succeeded/failed, plus unknown): call the PSP with our payment_id as its idempotency key; retryable errors and timeouts go to a backoff queue with a DLQ; webhooks and status queries settle unknowns
parts.why: ~2,400 PSP calls are in flight at peak (1,200/s × 2 s), so timeouts are routine. Writing the state before each call and reusing one key means a retry can only ever repeat the same charge request, which the PSP deduplicates.

parts.title: Double-entry ledger
parts.problem: Record every money movement (charge, fee, refund, payout) so that balances are provably correct, every cent is traceable, and history is never rewritten, for ~60M entries a day.

options.name: A mutable balance column per account
options.cons: no history; a bug silently corrupts money; nothing to audit

options.name: Single-entry transaction log
options.cons: no invariant to check: money can appear from nowhere

options.name: Double-entry append-only ledger; balances derived and cached
options.pros: every transaction balances (debits = credits); errors are visible; full audit trail
options.cons: more rows; corrections are new reversing entries, never edits

parts.choice: Double-entry, append-only ledger in its own Postgres: each transaction's debits equal its credits; posted from payment events by an idempotent poster; balances derived and cached per account
parts.why: N2 needs an invariant that can be checked mechanically: the sum of all entries is zero, per transaction and globally. 4.4 TB a year fits a partitioned Postgres; posting asynchronously keeps the PSP path fast, and a unique source_event_id makes posting exactly-once.

nodes.label: Payments DB: payments, idempotency keys, outbox

parts.title: Reconciliation with the processor
parts.problem: Our records, the ledger and the processor's settlement must agree to the cent. Find and resolve every mismatch caused by lost webhooks, bugs or processor errors.

options.name: Trust our own records
options.cons: a lost webhook or PSP error goes unnoticed until a merchant complains

options.name: Trust PSP webhooks in real time
options.cons: webhooks are lost, duplicated and reordered

options.name: Daily batch: match the PSP settlement file against the ledger, auto-fix known breaks, queue the rest
options.pros: catches every class of error; independent of the online path
options.cons: detects problems up to a day late

parts.choice: Daily reconciliation job: download the PSP settlement file to S3, match line by line with ledger entries by psp_ref and amount, post correcting entries for known break types, report the rest to finance
parts.why: ~10M lines a day is a small batch job. It is the only check that is independent of every online component, so it catches what idempotency and retries cannot (e.g. a charge the PSP made that we never recorded).

parts.title: Events and merchant webhooks via the outbox
parts.problem: Every state change must reach the ledger and the merchant's webhook exactly once in effect, even if the service crashes right after committing.

options.name: Write the DB, then publish to Kafka (dual write)
options.cons: a crash between the two loses or duplicates events

options.name: Transactional outbox + relay to Kafka; consumers idempotent by event id
options.pros: events commit atomically with state; at-least-once delivery with dedup
options.cons: a relay to run; a little latency

parts.choice: Transactional outbox in the payments DB, relayed to Kafka; the webhook dispatcher retries with backoff and signs each event; merchants dedupe by event id
parts.why: N1 applies to side effects too. The outbox makes 'state changed' and 'event exists' one commit; at-least-once delivery plus event ids is the honest guarantee to give merchants.
